why: N-Queens is the classic of pruning early: place one queen per row and reject a column the moment it shares a column or diagonal with an earlier queen, so whole subtrees of hopeless boards are never built.
hints: One queen per row is forced. So the only choice is which column the queen of each row takes. What makes a column illegal?
A queen at (r, c) attacks column c and the diagonals r - c and r + c. Keep three sets; only try columns absent from all three, recurse to the next row, then remove them.
Trying columns 0..n-1 in order at each row emits the solutions already sorted by their column vectors. Build each board as strings when row n is reached.
pitfalls: Checking the whole board at the end (instead of on placement) is far too slow.
n = 2 and n = 3 have no solution: return [].
Use r - c and r + c for the two diagonals, not just one.
